findings.title: Module include order stated both ways: State-before-Observables vs Observables-before-State
locations: PAGE: architecture, §4.9: "SimulationDomain → Observables → State → Cache → Forcing → Generator → Propagator → Particles → SimulationRun."
PAGE: api (overview): "submodules build on one another in the order SimulationDomain → State → Observables → Cache → …"
PAGE: Home, Components list: SimulationDomain, then State, then Observables, then Cache, …
PAGE: architecture, decision log (2026-08, user-directed): "The include order becomes State → Observables → Cache"
findings.contradicts: ARCHITECTURE.md §4.9's Layout summary (Observables before State) vs. the api-overview page, the Home page's component list, and the architecture decision log's own entry about this exact reordering (all three: State before Observables) — axis: relative include/dependency order of the State and Observables modules.
findings.description: Three independent current surfaces (api overview, Home page, and the decision log entry that made this exact change) agree State precedes Observables in the include order; ARCHITECTURE.md's own §4.9 'Layout summary' — a current-state section, not historical log text — states the opposite order. §4.9 reads as a stale leftover from before the 2026-08 'Observables precedes Cache' reordering decision was applied everywhere else.
findings.resolution_hint: Update §4.9's Layout summary line to 'SimulationDomain → State → Observables → Cache → …' to match the api page, Home page, and the decision log.

findings.title: Cache.particles_modified! hand-loop recipe omits the restart! call that Particles.restart! requires
locations: PAGE: api / Cache, particles_modified!: "A hand-run loop that repositions tracers itself must call this, then record_particle_velocities! to write the new values, and finally deposit_sample! to record them at the current epochs"
PAGE: api / Particles, restart!: "a hand-run loop that announces to the cache alone must call this as well, and a scheme carrying registers beyond that history is reached only this way"
findings.description: The Cache.particles_modified! docstring gives what reads as a complete three-step recipe for a hand-run loop repositioning tracers (particles_modified!, record_particle_velocities!, deposit_sample!), but never mentions restart!. Particles.restart!'s own docstring says a hand-run loop must call it too, since the Simulation-level particles_modified! form invokes it automatically but the bare-cache form cannot dispatch to it. A reader following only the more prominent Cache-page recipe would leave a multistep trajectory scheme's (e.g. AdamsBashforth) stale registers uncleared after a reposition.
findings.resolution_hint: Add a cross-reference/step to Cache.particles_modified!'s hand-loop recipe naming restart! for schemes with per-scheme registers beyond the cache's own sample history.

findings.title: StationarityCriterion keyword gate_skewness vs. internal field name gate_skew
locations: PAGE: api / SimulationRun, StationarityCriterion constructor: "gate_skewness = true"
Same page, Fields section: "gate_skew, min_turnovers, window_turnovers, tol and skew_floor all live inside monitor"
findings.description: Every other keyword in the constructor keeps its exact spelling in the Fields listing (min_turnovers, window_turnovers, tol, skew_floor), but gate_skewness is listed there as gate_skew. The docstring's disclaimer that 'the fields are not the keywords' could excuse this, but given every other name matches exactly, this one reads like an incomplete rename rather than a deliberate difference.
findings.resolution_hint: Either rename the internal field to gate_skewness for consistency, or state explicitly why this one keyword/field pair differs when none of its siblings do.

findings.title: ObservablesCache's shown constructor signature omits a keyword its own Arguments list documents
locations: PAGE: api / Cache — signature block: `ObservablesCache(domain; scalar = false, particle_velocities = nothing)`
PAGE: api / Cache — Arguments list, three lines later: '`history_depth = 1` — how many Lagrangian samples the run must be able to look back over'
findings.contradicts: The docstring's own shown call signature (2 keywords) vs its own Arguments prose (3 keywords, including history_depth) — same docstring.
findings.description: The literal constructor call shown for ObservablesCache has only `scalar` and `particle_velocities`, but the Arguments section right below documents a third real keyword, `history_depth = 1` (needed for the AdamsBashforth multistep particle scheme), with its own default and semantics. Every other constructor docstring in the corpus keeps its shown signature and Arguments list in lockstep; this looks like the signature line was never updated when multistep support was added.

findings.title: VarianceController's stated 'marginal law' divides by k instead of k_f, twice
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, VarianceController: 'The rate is the marginal law $A = \varepsilon/2k$ plus a proportional restoring term:' — immediately followed by a formula whose denominator is $2k_f(t)$
PAGE: architecture, §References, Bassenne et al. (2016) entry: 'the marginal law $A = \varepsilon/2k$ plus a proportional restoring term'
findings.contradicts: PAGE: architecture, decision log ('A state-dependent forcing rate belongs in the source...'): 'Its marginal term $\varepsilon/2k_f$ reinjects exactly what dissipation removes' — the correct denominator, k_f not k.
findings.description: Two surfaces (the VarianceController docstring's lead sentence and the References-list citation) state the marginal forcing law as A=eps/2k using the whole-field variance k, but the formula displayed one line later, its own explanatory sentence, and the decision log's record all use k_f (the forced band's variance). This is exactly the k-vs-k_f category error the decision log's own postscript says 'nearly shipped the wrong physics' — it has resurfaced in the prose describing the fix.

findings.title: StationarityCriterion's gate_skewness keyword silently becomes gate_skew as a field
locations: PAGE: api / SimulationRun, StationarityCriterion Arguments: '`gate_skewness` — also require the velocity-derivative skewness to have plateaued'
PAGE: api / SimulationRun, StationarityCriterion Fields: 'gate_skew, min_turnovers, window_turnovers, tol and skew_floor all live inside monitor'
findings.description: Every other keyword keeps its name as a field (min_turnovers, window_turnovers, tol, skew_floor, gate_scalar), but gate_skewness alone truncates to gate_skew with no stated reason, reading as an unexplained rename or leftover typo rather than a documented choice.

findings.title: particles_modified!(sim)'s effect on the particle scheme's own registers is asserted on one page, absent from its home docstring
locations: PAGE: api / Cache, particles_modified!: describes discarding the cache's own sample history and says the Simulation form 'announces the change to that run's cache' — no mention of the scheme's own buffers
PAGE: api / Particles, restart!: 'The Simulation form of particles_modified! calls this for you, after announcing the reposition to the observables cache'
findings.contradicts: Two docstrings for the same call, particles_modified!(sim), disagree on its scope — Cache's own docstring omits the restart! side-effect that Particles' page asserts it has.
findings.description: A reader who opens only Cache.particles_modified! (the natural place to look) cannot learn that the Simulation-form call also resets the trajectory scheme's own registers (e.g. an AdamsBashforth multistep history) via restart! — that fact appears only on the Particles page.

findings.title: Decision log claims the field- and particle-scheme keywords were unified to one word; the front door still uses two
locations: PAGE: architecture, decision log ('integrator → scheme on the binding'): 'The parameter pusher becomes scheme too, so one word names the same role on both sides of the run'
PAGE: api / SimulationRun, Simulation Arguments: 'scheme = IFLowStorageRK3()' (field scheme) and separately 'trajectory_scheme = EndpointHeun()' (particle scheme)
findings.contradicts: The decision log's 'one word... on both sides' claim vs the Simulation front door, which uses two distinct keyword names for the two kinds of scheme.
findings.description: At the low-level API (advect!, allocate_buffers) the particle scheme argument is indeed bare `scheme`, matching the decision. But at the Simulation front door — the surface most users meet first — the keyword is trajectory_scheme, presumably to avoid colliding with the field scheme's own `scheme` keyword, so the decision log's claim of full unification overstates the user-facing reality.

findings.title: The Sc = O(1) restriction is a load-bearing invariant absent from the architecture's own Invariants catalogue
locations: PAGE: api / SimulationRun, Simulation's schmidt argument: 'This package targets Sc = O(1) and carries no Batchelor-range machinery... Nothing enforces this — the value is accepted as given'

PAGE: architecture, §9 'Invariants — the deliberate absences': lists no-units, no-reimplemented-ops, no-privileged-precision, allocation-free, GPU-first, no-baked-in-closure, library-not-framework, phi-naming, deferred-futures — nothing about a Schmidt-number range
findings.contradicts: §9's own framing ('the public surface and these absences are the spec... a missing one usually encodes a decision') vs a real, unenforced restriction stated only in one keyword's prose elsewhere.
findings.description: Section 9 is explicitly where invariants are catalogued so a reader can trust the list is complete. The Sc-range restriction is exactly this kind of silent, unenforced invariant capable of quietly under-resolving a scalar field, yet it surfaces only inside the schmidt keyword's docstring prose, not in the dedicated invariants section a reader would check first.

findings.title: AdamsBashforth is shipped, but ARCHITECTURE.md/API-overview still claim a single fixed trajectory scheme
locations: PAGE architecture §4.6: "the trajectory scheme — today the single second-order `EndpointHeun`, with higher-order schemes the studied future axis"
PAGE api (overview) Particles bullet: "`Tracers`, second-order `advect!` (Heun-in-time)"
findings.contradicts: PAGE api/Particles, AbstractParticleIntegrator: "Two members today: `EndpointHeun`… and `AdamsBashforth`, a multistep method…" plus AdamsBashforth's full docstring, MultistepBuffers, the Simulation `trajectory_scheme` keyword, and its own decision-log entry — axis: is the higher-order scheme built or still future work?
findings.description: Architecture and the API overview assert in the present tense that EndpointHeun is the only trajectory scheme and a higher-order one is future work. AdamsBashforth is in fact fully implemented, documented, wired into Simulation, and cited by name in the decision log/references. A reader following the architecture-first reading path is told the wrong thing about a shipped capability.

findings.title: allocate_buffers's home docstring says "covers both" but a third call form exists
locations: PAGE api/Propagator, allocate_buffers: signatures list only (scheme,domain;scalar) and (scheme,tracers); text: "One generic covers both because it is one concept"
findings.contradicts: PAGE api/Particles, MultistepBuffers: "Build it with `allocate_buffers`(scheme, tracers, cache); a run builds it for you." — axis: two method signatures or three?
findings.description: The generic function's own home docstring, where the complete method list should live, documents two forms and explicitly says the generic covers 'both'. A third form allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers, cache), needed for AdamsBashforth's MultistepBuffers, is documented elsewhere but absent from and contradicted by the generic's own signature block.

findings.title: observables_cache.md's content table/cost analysis omit the Lagrangian sample-history slots
locations: PAGE observables_cache §2.4: "The table below lists the observables of this system, one row each." (no history row)
PAGE observables_cache §1.2–§1.4: derives cache contents/cost assuming single-valued deposits only
findings.contradicts: PAGE api/Cache, ObservablesCache Arguments/Fields: "history_depth = 1 — how many Lagrangian samples the run must be able to look back over…"; "particle_velocity_history … sample_steps … history_filled" — axis: is the sample history part of 'what the cache holds'?
findings.description: The design page purports to be the exhaustive statement of cache contents (§1–§2, not marked provisional) but predates the multistep trajectory scheme and was never updated when the cache grew a bounded ring buffer of past Lagrangian samples for AdamsBashforth. A reader reasoning about cache footprint or contents from this page misses an entire class of resident storage.

findings.title: StationarityCriterion's internal field is gate_skew, not gate_skewness, unexplained
locations: PAGE api/SimulationRun, StationarityCriterion Arguments: "`gate_skewness` — also require the velocity-derivative skewness…"
Same docstring, Fields: "gate_skew, min_turnovers, window_turnovers, tol and skew_floor all live inside monitor"
findings.contradicts: the same Fields list keeps gate_scalar identical to its keyword, so the keyword/field split is not applied uniformly — one sibling gate keeps its name, the other is silently truncated with no stated reason.
findings.description: The docstring frames field names as deliberately distinct from keywords, but the specific truncation gate_skewness→gate_skew reads like an unintentional shortening rather than a considered rename, especially since the sibling gate_scalar crosses the same field/keyword boundary unchanged.

findings.title: Notation's "deposit" entry attributes the particle-velocity write to "the tracer advance," contradicting record_particle_velocities! elsewhere
locations: PAGE notation, Vocabulary "deposit": "the tracer advance writes, deposit_sample! marks"
PAGE notation, Vocabulary "iteration": "…advance any tracers and record their sample" (treats advance and record as separate actions)
findings.contradicts: PAGE api/Particles, record_particle_velocities!: "This call is that slot's only producer of values… Interpolate here, then mark current there."; PAGE api/Cache, deposit_sample!: "record_particle_velocities! writes, this call records." — axis: which verb writes, advect! or record_particle_velocities!?
findings.description: The notation page's own 'iteration' entry treats advancing tracers (advect!) and recording their sample (record_particle_velocities!) as distinct sequential actions, yet the 'deposit' entry two lines away uses 'the tracer advance' to mean the write that every other page attributes specifically to record_particle_velocities!. Since the page claims to fix vocabulary precisely, this reads as an internal slip.

findings.title: Two different numeric conventions for "the large-eddy turnover time" coexist unreconciled
locations: PAGE api/Forcing, VarianceController Arguments: "turnover_time … taken as 2k∞/3ε∞"
PAGE architecture §2: "the eddy-turnover clock Δt ε/k" (implying turnover time k/ε)
findings.contradicts: no page states the two are the same quantity, but both are introduced as THE turnover/eddy-turnover time-scale with no cross-reference reconciling the differing 2/3 prefactor (u'^2/ε vs k/ε) — axis: is the large-eddy turnover time k/ε or (2/3)k/ε?
findings.description: Both are legitimate, differently-normalized turbulence conventions, so this may be intentional, but neither page flags the distinction; a reader conflating StationarityCriterion's turnover bookkeeping with VarianceController's default turnover_time would silently pick up a 2/3 factor. Flagged at low confidence since it may be a deliberate, unlabeled difference rather than an error.

findings.title: Generator page contradicts itself on how PhaseShift's velocity reuse is tracked
locations: PAGE api/Generator, ResolvedGenerator docstring: "recorded as the identity of the û it was taken of rather than either signature"
PAGE api/Generator, scalar_rhs! docstring: "displaced_velocity_current = false" / "Pass displaced_velocity_current = true only if nothing has changed"
findings.description: One passage says the same-stage velocity-reuse optimization is auto-tracked by comparing a recorded û identity, so a caller can never get it wrong ('finding it stale rebuilds the recovery itself'). The other passage, on the same page, shows scalar_rhs! taking an explicit caller-supplied Bool keyword that is blindly trusted, where getting it wrong would be 'quietly wrong'. These describe two different correctness postures for what is claimed to be one mechanism.
findings.contradicts: ResolvedGenerator's field docs describe automatic identity-based freshness detection ('rather than either signature'); scalar_rhs!'s own signature is exactly such a signature parameter, manually asserted by the caller with no described automatic check.
findings.resolution_hint: Clarify whether the callee actually compares û identity (making the keyword redundant/advisory) or whether the keyword is load-bearing and the 'rather than either signature' phrasing is stale.

findings.title: ObservablesCache's shown constructor signature omits its own documented history_depth keyword
locations: PAGE api/Cache: "ObservablesCache(domain; scalar = false, particle_velocities = nothing)"
PAGE api/Cache, Arguments: "history_depth = 1 — how many Lagrangian samples the run must be able to look back over"
findings.description: The printed call signature for ObservablesCache shows only two keywords, but the Arguments section immediately below documents a third, history_depth, with its own default and rationale for multistep tracer schemes. A reader who copies the shown signature would not know this keyword exists.
findings.contradicts: The signature block and the Arguments list of the same docstring disagree about what the constructor accepts.
findings.resolution_hint: Add history_depth to the shown signature.

findings.title: allocate_buffers's documented return-type contract is falsified by AdamsBashforth's MultistepBuffers
locations: PAGE api/Propagator, allocate_buffers docstring: "allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers) -> ParticleIntegratorBuffers"
PAGE api/Particles, MultistepBuffers docstring: "Build it with allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers, cache)"
Decision log: "one generic across both sides, because it is one concept"
findings.description: allocate_buffers's own (home) docstring documents exactly two methods and states the particle-side one always returns ParticleIntegratorBuffers. A third method exists, taking a third argument (cache) for AdamsBashforth, and returns a structurally different type, MultistepBuffers, which merely nests a ParticleIntegratorBuffers for its bootstrap phase. A caller reading only the canonical docstring cannot discover this method or its differing arity/return type.
findings.contradicts: The decision log's claim that allocate_buffers is 'one generic... because it is one concept' returning one type, versus the actual third method with a different arity and a different return type.
findings.resolution_hint: Document the third method on allocate_buffers's own docstring, or reconsider whether MultistepBuffers should be presented as returned by a genuinely uniform interface.

findings.title: Particles module docstring (the map) is stale relative to its own page
locations: PAGE api/Particles, module docstring: "AbstractParticleIntegrator, EndpointHeun — the trajectory time-integration schemes"
Same page: AdamsBashforth, MultistepBuffers, restart!, history_depth are each documented, and all appear in the top-level Index
findings.description: The module map still names only one trajectory-scheme family member and omits four names (AdamsBashforth, MultistepBuffers, restart!, history_depth) that are fully documented later on the very same page and listed in the Index. This is the doc corpus's own 'current & complete' rule failing on its own module map.
findings.resolution_hint: Add the four missing names to the module docstring's bullet list.

findings.title: The same staleness recurs on the Home and api-overview pages
locations: PAGE Home, Components: "second-order advection and field sampling along trajectories"
PAGE api (overview): "second-order advect! (Heun-in-time)"
findings.description: Both pages still frame particle tracking as strictly second-order, with no mention of the higher-order AdamsBashforth alternative documented elsewhere on the site — the same staleness class as Finding about Particles's module docstring, recurring across three separate pages, suggesting the addition of the second trajectory scheme swept type/function docstrings but not summary prose.
findings.resolution_hint: Update the summary prose on both pages alongside the module docstring fix.

findings.title: particles_modified! gets a Simulation-convenience overload; its stated counterpart fields_modified! does not
locations: PAGE api/Cache, particles_modified!: "particles_modified!(cache)\nparticles_modified!(sim)", "mirroring deposit!'s two forms"
PAGE api/Cache, fields_modified!: "fields_modified!(cache)" (only form shown)
findings.description: particles_modified! explicitly calls itself 'the particle counterpart of fields_modified!', yet only particles_modified! gets a second, Simulation-taking overload. A user who reseeds the velocity on a live Simulation must drill into sim.cache; a user who repositions tracers gets a direct convenience call. Nothing explains the asymmetry between two functions presented as mirrors of one another.
findings.contradicts: particles_modified!'s docstring calling itself the counterpart of fields_modified! versus the two functions actually exposing a different number of call forms.
findings.resolution_hint: Add a fields_modified!(sim) overload, or explain why particles_modified! alone needs one.

findings.title: "One word... on both sides of the run" is not what the Simulation front door actually does
locations: Decision log: "The parameter pusher becomes scheme too, so one word names the same role on both sides of the run."
PAGE api/SimulationRun, Simulation Arguments: "scheme = IFLowStorageRK3()" and "trajectory_scheme = EndpointHeun()"
findings.description: The claim holds at the lower-level function signatures (advect!(scheme, ...), allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers)). But the one place the field and particle schemes coexist in a single flat namespace — the Simulation front door — in fact uses two different keywords, necessarily, to avoid a collision. The decision log's blanket wording does not record this front-door exception.
findings.contradicts: Decision log's 'one word names the same role on both sides of the run' versus Simulation's distinct scheme / trajectory_scheme keywords.
findings.resolution_hint: Note the front-door disambiguation explicitly in the decision log or the Simulation docstring.

findings.title: ParticleIntegratorBuffers's name implies a generality it doesn't have
locations: PAGE api/Particles, module docstring: "ParticleIntegratorBuffers the per-step storage each one needs"
PAGE api/Particles, MultistepBuffers docstring: field "startup — the ParticleIntegratorBuffers the bootstrap EndpointHeun steps use"
findings.description: The module map frames ParticleIntegratorBuffers as the per-scheme storage type ('each one needs'), suggesting a family-wide role parallel to the field side's IntegratorBuffers. It is actually specific to EndpointHeun; a second scheme (AdamsBashforth) requires an entirely differently-named type (MultistepBuffers) that merely embeds the first by composition rather than extending or sharing it.
findings.resolution_hint: Either rename toward the concrete scheme it actually serves, or restructure so the two scheme buffer types share a visible common shape.

findings.title: FlowConditions and FlowParameters are a naming-collision risk the docs must explicitly defuse
locations: PAGE api/Generator, FlowConditions docstring: "Not to be confused with Phenomenology's FlowParameters, which shares two field names"
findings.description: FlowConditions (what a run is configured with) and FlowParameters (what a run has been measured to have) sit one word apart, in modules a user crosses between routinely via flow_parameters(sim), and share field names. That the docs must spend a sentence warning readers not to confuse the two is itself evidence of a naming smell, even though the underlying conceptual distinction is sound.
findings.resolution_hint: Consider a more distinct name for one of the pair.

findings.title: prepare_forcing! breaks the 'return the mutated argument' convention its three sibling hooks follow
locations: PAGE api/Forcing, AbstractForcing docstring: "Each mutating hook returns its mutated argument (set_forcing_rate! the rate, add_forcing_source! the right-hand side, project_forcing! the field); prepare_forcing! returns nothing."
findings.description: Three of the four lifecycle hooks return the argument they mutate; prepare_forcing! also mutates something (the forcing's own internal state, held on its first argument) yet is the one hook that returns nothing instead of forcing. The asymmetry is stated as fact with no stated reason, in an interface whose whole point is a uniform four-hook contract.
findings.resolution_hint: Either justify the asymmetry or have prepare_forcing! return forcing like its siblings.

findings.title: Simulation's front door is a ~20-keyword flat constructor spanning unrelated concerns
locations: PAGE api/SimulationRun, Simulation(; grid_points_per_axis, κ_max_η = nothing, kinetic_energy = 1.5, side_length = 2π, element_type = Float64, array_type = Array, dealiasing = TwoThirds(), kwargs...)
findings.description: The front door's keyword surface spans grid/precision, two independent forcing choices, particle count and scheme, initial-condition shape, a CFL override, and RNG — roughly twenty independent settings in one flat namespace, including a runtime-validated mutually exclusive pair (viscosity vs. κ_max_η). This is a deliberate, documented ergonomic choice and not itself re-litigated here, but its breadth is a plausible contributing factor to the signature/arity drifts found elsewhere (history_depth, allocate_buffers) going unnoticed.
findings.resolution_hint: Consider grouping related keywords into small option bundles if the surface keeps growing.

findings.title: "The marginal law A = ε/2k" contradicts VarianceController's own formula (whole-field k vs band k_f)
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, §Forcing strategies, VarianceController — "The rate is the marginal law $A = \varepsilon/2k$ plus a proportional restoring term"
PAGE: api / Forcing, same docstring display — "$A(\boldsymbol{\kappa}, t) = \frac{\varepsilon(t) - G[k(t) - k_\infty]/t_\ell}{2k_f(t)}$"
PAGE: architecture, §References, Bassenne entry — "the marginal law $A = \varepsilon/2k$ plus a proportional restoring term"
findings.contradicts: PAGE: decisions, the VarianceController entry — "Its marginal term $\varepsilon/2k_f$ reinjects exactly what dissipation removes"; and PAGE: architecture §7 — "$\langle f, f\rangle$ for the variance the controller holds, $\langle f, b\,f\rangle$ for the band it normalizes by". Axis: which variance normalizes the marginal rate.
findings.description: The forcing acts only in the band, so dk/dt = 2A·k_f. Only A = ε/(2k_f) reinjects exactly ε; A = ε/2k injects ε·k_f/k, and the exponential-relaxation claim dk/dt = −G(k−k_∞)/t_ℓ stated three lines below fails with it. This is the exact k-vs-k_f swap the decision log records as having "nearly shipped the wrong physics" — a category error between the quantity a forcing acts on and the quantity it holds — now sitting in the prose of two rendered surfaces.
findings.resolution_hint: Write the marginal law as A = ε/(2k_f) on both surfaces, or qualify it as Bassenne's whole-field form that becomes ε/(2k_f) for a banded drive.

findings.title: The large-scale roll-off length wears three glyphs: ℓ, L, and L₁₁
locations: PAGE: notation, §Derived scales — "$\ell$ | the length a large-scale roll-off is evaluated against … never the box side $L$"
PAGE: notation, §Numerics — "$L$ | box side ($\Omega = [0,L)^3$)"
PAGE: api / phenomenology / Spectra, ModelSpectrum — "reads $\varepsilon$ and the roll-off's own length $L$"
PAGE: api / phenomenology / Spectra, large_scale_length — "related by $\ell_{11}/\ell_{0} = C_\varepsilon (2/3)^{3/2}$"
findings.contradicts: ModelSpectrum's "the roll-off's own length $L$" against the glossary's "$\ell$ … never the box side $L$" and "$L$ | box side"; and ℓ₁₁ against the glossary's L₁₁ for one and the same longitudinal integral scale.
findings.description: The glossary introduces ℓ precisely so the roll-off length is not read as the box side, then ModelSpectrum calls that length L in prose while its own display formula writes f_L(κℓ). Separately the longitudinal integral scale is L₁₁ in the glossary, Observables and FlowParameters but ℓ₁₁ on the Spectra page. One concept, three glyphs — and one of them is the symbol most likely to be misread as the box side.
findings.resolution_hint: Use ℓ for the roll-off length everywhere on the Spectra page and L₁₁ for the integral scale; never L for anything but the box side.

findings.title: "Four strategies are provided", then five are described
locations: PAGE: architecture, §4.4 — "Four strategies are provided. `NoForcing` (free decay) and `Linear` …"
PAGE: architecture, §4.4, same paragraph — "because these four methods are written through tensor-order-generic field operators"
findings.contradicts: PAGE: api / Forcing, module map, which lists five strategies: NoForcing, Linear, ConstantPower, VarianceController, VarianceRescaling — all five also named in the §4.4 paragraph itself.
findings.description: The count was not updated when VarianceController became the default (recorded in the decision log). Five strategies are then named under a sentence that says four, and "these four methods" a few lines later is ambiguous between the strategies and the four lifecycle hooks. A reader counting the menu against the sentence finds them disagreeing.
findings.resolution_hint: Say "Five strategies are provided" and disambiguate "these four methods" to "these strategies".

findings.title: The eddy-turnover time is defined two ways: k/ε and 2k/3ε
locations: PAGE: api / SimulationRun, StationarityCriterion — "which normalizes the eddy-turnover clock $\Delta t \varepsilon/k$"
PAGE: api / Forcing, VarianceController Arguments — "the large-eddy turnover time $t_\ell$. When omitted it is taken as $2k_\infty/3\varepsilon_\infty$"
findings.contradicts: The two quantities both named a turnover time differ by 3/2 (k/ε versus u'²/ε). Axis: the definition of the large-eddy turnover time.
findings.description: run!, the observables-cache page and the stationarity criterion all clock turnovers as Δt·ε/k, i.e. T = k/ε; the controller's default settling scale is 2k/(3ε). Both are defensible conventions, but the package's rule is one value per concept, and min_turnovers / window_turnovers are stated in units the controller does not share. Mitigating: the controller notes only t_ℓ/G is observable, so the factor is absorbed by the gain.
findings.resolution_hint: Fix T = k/ε in the notation glossary and either adopt it for t_ℓ's default or name the controller's default u'²/ε explicitly.

findings.title: VarianceRescaling summarized as holding "a band's amplitude", which over = :total does not do
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, module map — "`VarianceRescaling` — hold a band's amplitude by deterministic rescaling, at first order."
PAGE: api / Forcing, VarianceRescaling — "`:total` rescales the band to absorb the whole-field deficit, so the whole-field value equals `target`"
findings.contradicts: The map asserts the band is the held quantity; the type docstring makes the held quantity a required, undefaulted choice between band and whole field. Axis: what is held versus what is rescaled.
findings.description: The one-liner states as fact the very thing the type refuses to default, and the distinction is load-bearing: the docstring says over "decides which quantity a run may no longer measure", and grid-mode calibration depends on the whole-field reading. Linear's one-liner ("a fixed linear rate on a band") is the right shape — name the mechanism, not one of the two possible targets.
findings.resolution_hint: "Hold a band's or the whole field's L² observable by deterministic rescaling of the band, at first order."

findings.title: VarianceController alone carries a band kernel yet takes no domain and has no deferred form
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, VarianceController — "VarianceController(; target, gain = 1, turnover_time = nothing, lowest_shell = 1, highest_shell = 2)" with field "`band` — the band-pass kernel, lazy"
PAGE: api / Forcing, ConstantPower — "ConstantPower(domain; injection_rate, …)" with the same field "`band` — the band-pass kernel, lazy"
PAGE: api / Forcing, DeferredForcing — the operator-free list gives Linear, ConstantPower, VarianceRescaling only
findings.contradicts: ConstantPower needs a FixedDomain to build a lazy band kernel; VarianceController documents the same lazy band kernel with no domain argument anywhere in its construction path.
findings.description: Every other banded strategy is built on a FixedDomain and has a DeferredForcing twin; the default velocity forcing has neither, yet documents the same lazy band kernel its domain-taking sibling builds from wavenumbers. Either the domain argument is vestigial on ConstantPower or it is missing here — the pages do not say which, and a reader assembling a run by hand cannot tell how the controller learns its shells' wavenumbers.
findings.resolution_hint: State on VarianceController why no domain is needed (the kernel is a domain-free radial symbol materialized at apply time), and say whether ConstantPower's domain is still required.

findings.title: Two measured CatmullRom interpolation floors that the stated Δx^(d+1) scaling cannot reconcile
locations: PAGE: api / Particles, EndpointHeun — "a degree-$d$ interpolant's trajectory floor falls as $\Delta x^{d+1}$ … at $N = 128$, floor $1\times10^{-5}$"
PAGE: decisions, the Adams–Bashforth entry — "Measured on a frozen ABC flow at $64^3$, $T = 1$: `CatmullRom` ($C^1$, degree 2) floors at $1.2\times10^{-5}$"
findings.contradicts: A degree-2 floor ∝ Δx³ should fall about eightfold from N = 64 to N = 128 (1.2e−5 → ~1.5e−6); the quoted N = 128 floor is 1e−5, essentially unchanged. Axis: the measured floor's resolution scaling.
findings.description: The two measurements use different test fields (a frozen ABC flow versus "a band-limited field"), which may explain the gap, but neither page says so. As rendered, the pair reads as contradicting the scaling law both cite, and a reader sizing an interpolation choice from these numbers would draw opposite conclusions depending on which page they landed on.
findings.resolution_hint: Name the test field beside each number, or quote both floors from one study.

findings.title: Density-vs-sum and rate-vs-quantity slips in the notation tables
locations: PAGE: notation, §Diagnostics — "$E_\varphi(\kappa)$ | the scalar-variance spectrum, summing to $\langle\varphi^{2}\rangle$"
PAGE: notation, §Diagnostics, adjacent rows — "$E(\kappa)$ … $k = \int_0^\infty E(\kappa)\,\mathrm{d}\kappa$" and "$E_n$ … so $k = \sum_n E_n$"
PAGE: notation, §Forcing — "$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{target}}$ | the injection rate a ConstantPower holds: energy for the velocity, scalar variance for the scalar"
findings.contradicts: The page's own discriminator — a density integrates, a per-shell energy sums — is applied to E(κ) and E_n but broken one row later for E_φ(κ), which is declared a function of κ yet said to sum.
findings.description: E_φ(κ) is a per-unit-wavenumber density (its own row makes κ the argument) but is glossed with "summing to", the verb the table reserves for the measured per-shell E_n. In the forcing row an injection rate is glossed with two quantities ("energy", "scalar variance"); the ConstantPower docstring gets it right ("the rate at which energy … is injected"). Both are the density/energy and rate/quantity confusions the architecture names as their own correctness class.
findings.resolution_hint: "integrating to ⟨φ²⟩"; and "the rate at which energy (velocity) or scalar variance (scalar) is injected".

findings.title: Li2008 names a paper for a constant the package fitted itself
locations: PAGE: api / phenomenology / Scalings, Li2008 — "The value is this package's own reduction of the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (JHTDB) … dataset"
PAGE: architecture, §4.8 — "the paper is the author-year handle (`Pope2000`, first author's surname…)"
PAGE: api / phenomenology / Scalings, Sreenivasan1995 — "the consensus value as quoted by Sagaut & Cambon (2018), not a figure read off the 1995 paper"
findings.contradicts: The stated three-level naming rule binds the author-year handle to the paper the parametrization is taken from; G ≈ 0.9 is not published in Li et al. (2008), which published the dataset.
findings.description: Two presets carry an author-year handle for a coefficient that paper does not contain. Both disclose it honestly in prose, so this is a naming-rule question rather than a misattribution — but a run's viscosity is set from Li2008's G, and provenance(law) is what a validation comparison cites, so the handle is what a reader will report as the source of the number.
findings.resolution_hint: Either state the exception in the naming rule ("a handle may name the dataset a fit was reduced from") or carry the package's own fit under its own handle with the dataset cited in the Reference.

findings.title: ObservablesCache documents a history_depth keyword its signature does not show
locations: PAGE: api / Cache, ObservablesCache signature — "ObservablesCache(domain; scalar = false, particle_velocities = nothing)"
PAGE: api / Cache, same docstring Arguments — "`history_depth = 1` — how many Lagrangian samples the run must be able to look back over"
findings.contradicts: The rendered signature omits a keyword the Arguments list documents and the Fields list depends on (particle_velocity_history), and which the exported Particles.history_depth exists to supply.
findings.description: A reader following the signature cannot build a cache for an AdamsBashforth run; a reader following the Arguments passes a keyword the signature says does not exist. The multistep trajectory scheme is a shipped, documented option, so this is the live construction path for it.
findings.resolution_hint: Add history_depth = 1 to the rendered signature line.

findings.title: The eddy-turnover clock is load-bearing on four surfaces but bound in no glossary
locations: PAGE: api / SimulationRun, run! — "an eddy-turnover budget accumulates $\Delta t \varepsilon/k$ from the observables it computes"
PAGE: notation, §Vocabulary — entries for iteration, deposit, slot, epoch, register, front door, observation, chart, resolved; none for turnover
findings.description: The turnover is the unit of min_turnovers, window_turnovers and max_turnovers and appears on run!, StationarityCriterion, warmup! and the cache page, yet neither the symbol table nor the vocabulary table defines it. Given the competing 2k/3ε of the VarianceController default, one glossary row fixing T = k/ε would settle both this and that ambiguity.
findings.resolution_hint: Add a §Diagnostics or §Vocabulary row: turnover time T = k/ε, the clock a budget accumulates as Δt·ε/k.

findings.title: "Two registers per field" for IFLowStorageRK3 means different things on two pages
locations: PAGE: architecture §4.5: "three spectral registers per field against the low-storage scheme's two, counting the same way on both sides: the scheme's own registers plus the dealiasing seam's assembly register"

PAGE: api / Propagator, IFLowStorageRK3: "two field registers per field: the state's own array plus one accumulator (stage1)... The IntegratorBuffers a run allocates can hold more than that count — for this scheme it adds nonlinear"
findings.contradicts: Architecture's 'two' = stage1+nonlinear (excludes state array); Propagator's 'two' (Williamson 2N convention) = state+stage1 (excludes nonlinear). Both land on the numeral 2 for the same scheme via two different pairs drawn from the same three underlying arrays.
findings.description: Not a numerical error — both pages agree IFRK2 costs exactly one more register than IFLowStorageRK3 under either convention, and Propagator's docstring does flag its own count differs from IntegratorBuffers' real contents. But a reader comparing the bare numeral 'two' across the two pages without reading both caveats closely could reasonably think they're the same claim.

findings.title: Predictor register is prefixed on the velocity side, bare on the scalar side
locations: PAGE: api / Propagator, IntegratorBuffers Fields: "stage2, velocity_predictor_spectral" (top level, velocity) vs "stage2 and predictor_spectral (IFRK2's corrector register and predictor state φ̂*)" (nested ScalarBuffers)
findings.description: stage1/stage2/nonlinear are unprefixed at both the top (velocity) level and inside ScalarBuffers, but the analogous predictor register is velocity_predictor_spectral at top level and bare predictor_spectral inside ScalarBuffers — the one field in the set that breaks the otherwise-consistent prefix pattern.

findings.title: Two CatmullRom interpolation-floor numbers are suspiciously close across different stated experiments
locations: PAGE: api / Particles, EndpointHeun: "at N = 128, floor 1×10⁻⁵ against time error 6×10⁻⁵" (band-limited field)
PAGE: decisions (2026-08, second trajectory scheme): "Measured on a frozen ABC flow at 64³, T=1: CatmullRom (C¹, degree 2) floors at 1.2×10⁻⁵"
findings.contradicts: Same interpolation floor for the same scheme (CatmullRom) reported as ~1e-5 at N=128 on one field and ~1.2e-5 at N=64 on a different (ABC) flow — plausibly two genuinely independent measurements that happen to be close, but close enough, with mismatched grid sizes, to warrant a second look.
findings.description: Could be entirely legitimate (interpolation floor depending mainly on spectral content, not resolution) but the near-coincidence plus a swapped-looking N (128 vs 64) is worth the package owner double-checking against source rather than the panel asserting it as safe.

findings.title: IFRK2's CFL margin is an unguarded, Reynolds-number-blind constant
locations: PAGE: api / Propagator, recommended_cfl: "its 0.25 is an empirical margin rather than a computed limit... The same 0.25 is returned at every Reynolds number while the viscous damping it rests on weakens as ν falls, and there is no code-level guard for this."
findings.description: Already disclosed, not hidden, so not a documentation defect per se — flagged only because a performance/stability-focused reviewer would want on record that IFRK2 at high Reynolds number with the default cfl is a documented but entirely unguarded footgun (no runtime check backs the user-facing warning).

findings.title: ObservablesCache's own signature omits a keyword its own Arguments list documents
locations: PAGE: api / Cache — "ObservablesCache(domain; scalar = false, particle_velocities = nothing)"
PAGE: api / Cache, Arguments — "history_depth = 1 — how many Lagrangian samples the run must be able to look back over, including the current one."
findings.description: The docstring's own top-of-page signature line lists only `scalar` and `particle_velocities` as keywords, but the same docstring's Arguments section documents a third keyword, `history_depth = 1`, as if it belonged to that same constructor call. This is a self-contradiction within one docstring, not a cross-page drift: a reader cannot tell whether `history_depth` is a real, missing-from-the-signature keyword (needed to size the multistep sample history for `AdamsBashforth`) or stale prose left over from an earlier revision.
findings.contradicts: Same docstring, two sections: the code-block signature vs. the Arguments bullet list, over whether `history_depth` is a constructor keyword.
findings.resolution_hint: Add `history_depth = 1` to the signature line if it is real, or delete the Arguments bullet if it is stale.

findings.title: allocate_buffers's home docstring enumerates two forms; MultistepBuffers invokes an undocumented third
locations: PAGE: api / Propagator, allocate_buffers — "allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers) -> ParticleIntegratorBuffers" and "One generic covers both"
PAGE: api / Particles, MultistepBuffers — "Build it with allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers, cache); a run builds it for you."
findings.description: allocate_buffers's own docstring presents itself as exhaustive — exactly two forms, explicitly claiming 'one generic covers both' the field and particle sides. MultistepBuffers's docstring (built for AdamsBashforth) requires a third, 3-argument form (scheme, tracers, cache) returning a different type, which never appears on allocate_buffers's own page. A reader following the 'one docstring per operation, on the bare binding' convention would never learn this form exists.
findings.contradicts: allocate_buffers docstring (PAGE: api / Propagator) claims two forms and completeness; MultistepBuffers docstring (PAGE: api / Particles) uses a third form of the same generic.
findings.resolution_hint: Add the 3-argument form to allocate_buffers's own docstring.

findings.title: Phenomenology's roll-off-factor pieces are positional-only, contradicting the module's stated 'every preset is keyword' rule
locations: PAGE: api / phenomenology / Spectra, module docstring — "Every preset is a type with a keyword constructor, invoked as Name(; …)."

PAGE: api / phenomenology / Spectra — "PopeLargeScale(c_L, p₀)", "PopeDissipation(c_η, β)", "VonKarmanLarge(c_L)", "PaoDissipation(α)", "ExponentialDissipation(β)" — each shown only as a bare positional signature, no keyword form, no defaults
findings.description: Every named law in Scalings, StructureFunctions, and the EnergySpectrum/ScalarSpectrum presets (Sreenivasan1998, Kolmogorov1941, Pope2000, ObukhovCorrsin1949, ...) is keyword-constructed with defaults, matching the module's blanket claim. The five roll-off-factor pieces those presets are literally composed from (their fitted coefficients are the exact numbers a one-level-up preset exposes as defaulted keywords) are documented with only a positional constructor and no defaults at all — an arity split between two families in the same module with no stated rule, and no way to override one coefficient without naming the others positionally in order.
findings.contradicts: Module docstring's 'every preset is a type with a keyword constructor' vs. the roll-off-factor docstrings' positional-only signatures.
findings.resolution_hint: Either give the roll-off factors keyword forms with defaults, or state explicitly why 'preset' excludes them and the positional convention is deliberate.

findings.title: VarianceController is the only forcing missing the domain-taking / DeferredForcing pair its siblings all have
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, DeferredForcing — "The operator-free keyword constructors Linear(; rate, …) / ConstantPower(; injection_rate, …) / VarianceRescaling(; target, over, …) each return a DeferredForcing ... materialized ... once the FixedDomain exists"

PAGE: api / Forcing, VarianceController — "VarianceController(; target, gain = 1, turnover_time = nothing, lowest_shell = 1, highest_shell = 2)", its only documented constructor, with Fields including 'band — the band-pass kernel'
findings.description: Linear, ConstantPower, and VarianceRescaling each show a domain-taking constructor plus an operator-free DeferredForcing twin, and DeferredForcing's docstring names exactly these three as the family with that shape. VarianceController — the package's default velocity forcing — appears everywhere with only the keyword-only form and is absent from that enumeration, yet it has a 'band' field structurally identical to ConstantPower's (which needs domain-derived shell geometry to build). Either VarianceController is quietly deferred too and belongs in the list, or it genuinely builds its band with no domain and the doc never says why it alone can.
findings.contradicts: DeferredForcing's three-member enumeration of forcings with a domain-taking/deferred pair vs. VarianceController's single, domain-free constructor and its domain-shaped band field.
findings.resolution_hint: State explicitly whether VarianceController needs no domain at construction and why, or add its missing domain-taking form.

findings.title: Particle-buffer types split into two names where the field-side analogue keeps one
locations: PAGE: api / Propagator, IntegratorBuffers — "Built per scheme by allocate_buffers... An array another scheme would use is left nothing, never allocated" (one type, both schemes)
PAGE: api / Particles, ParticleIntegratorBuffers (fields predictor/predictor_points/velocity_predictor, EndpointHeun-only) vs. MultistepBuffers ("the per-scheme registers of an AdamsBashforth")
findings.description: On the field side, IFLowStorageRK3 and IFRK2 share one buffer type, IntegratorBuffers, with unused fields nulled. On the particle side, EndpointHeun and AdamsBashforth get two differently-named buffer types, and the generically-named one (ParticleIntegratorBuffers) turns out to be EndpointHeun-specific (it is even reused internally as MultistepBuffers's own bootstrap scratch) while the truly generic role is served by a type named after one scheme's mechanism. No rule explains why the two sides of the identical per-scheme-scratch pattern diverge in naming strategy.
findings.resolution_hint: Either rename for parallelism (e.g. a scheme-parametrized family) or state the reason one side merges and the other splits.

findings.title: particles_modified!(cache) and particles_modified!(sim) are not interchangeable, with no cache-only full reset
locations: PAGE: api / Particles, restart! — "Its bare-cache form clears the sample history the cache itself holds, but cannot dispatch here ... a scheme carrying registers beyond that history is reached only this way."
findings.description: The two documented overloads of particles_modified! look like the same 'two forms to reach for' pattern used elsewhere (e.g. deposit!), but they are not equivalent: only the sim form also resets a multistep scheme's registers via restart!. A hand-rolled loop driving Tracers directly with AdamsBashforth and only a bare ObservablesCache has no single call that fully invalidates state after a reposition, and the cache-only form gives no signal that anything is left undone.
findings.resolution_hint: Either add a cache+buffers overload, or have particles_modified!(cache) warn/return a sentinel when a scheme with extra registers is in play.

findings.title: Kolmogorov1962 does not disclose which StructureFunction evaluator it lacks, unlike its sibling SheLeveque1994
locations: PAGE: api / phenomenology / StructureFunctions, SheLeveque1994 — "It predicts exponents, not amplitudes, so it implements scaling_exponent but not structure_function."
PAGE: api / phenomenology / StructureFunctions, Kolmogorov1962 — documents only scaling_exponent(law; order), with no statement about structure_function support
findings.description: Kolmogorov1962 and SheLeveque1994 are the same shape of law — both intermittency models giving only an anomalous exponent, no amplitude law. The StructureFunction family's whole public contract is its two evaluators (structure_function, scaling_exponent), so which one a given law implements is exactly the fact a cold reader needs. SheLeveque1994 states it explicitly; Kolmogorov1962's docstring is silent, leaving structure_function support undocumented by omission for a law of identical shape.
findings.contradicts: SheLeveque1994's explicit disclosure of its missing evaluator vs. Kolmogorov1962's silence on the same question for the same law shape.
findings.resolution_hint: Add the same disclosure sentence to Kolmogorov1962 (or state why it differs).

findings.title: VarianceController's divide-by-band-variance has no documented floor, unlike the identical hazard in ConstantPower
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, ConstantPower — "An empty band is left alone, not driven infinitely hard ... Below a small floor on E_band the amplitude is set to zero."
PAGE: api / Forcing, VarianceController — rate law A(κ,t) = [ε(t) − G(k(t) − k_∞)/t_ℓ] / (2 k_f(t)), no equivalent statement about k_f → 0
findings.description: ConstantPower's rate divides by the forced band's own observable, and its docstring names the empty-band floor that prevents a divide-by-near-zero kick. VarianceController's rate has the identical structural hazard (k_f(t) in the denominator) and is the package's default forcing, yet its docstring states no analogous guard or floor. Either the protection exists silently for the default forcing of all of them, or the family's stated safety property is not actually uniform across its members.
findings.resolution_hint: State VarianceController's behavior as k_f → 0, matching ConstantPower's disclosure.

findings.title: "Four strategies are provided" enumerates five
locations: PAGE: architecture §4.4: "Four strategies are provided. `NoForcing`... `Linear`... `ConstantPower`... `VarianceController`... `VarianceRescaling`..."
PAGE: architecture §4.4 (same paragraph): "because these four methods are written through tensor-order-generic field operators"
PAGE: api / Forcing (module docstring): "NoForcing... Linear... ConstantPower... VarianceController... VarianceRescaling" (five strategies, no miscount)
findings.contradicts: Architecture's own sentence names five forcing strategies (NoForcing, Linear, ConstantPower, VarianceController, VarianceRescaling) while asserting the count is four (twice in the same paragraph); the Forcing API page and the Home page independently list the same five with no such error.
findings.description: The set is the built, non-archived forcing strategies. Architecture §4.4 states cardinality 'Four' twice, then itself enumerates five (StochasticOU is explicitly archived, so it cannot be the missing fifth). Almost certainly a stale count left from before VarianceController was added as a strategy (per the decision log, it later became the default). 5 of 5 enumerated members contradict the stated count of 4.

findings.title: "the single EndpointHeun" vs "Two members today"
locations: PAGE: architecture §4.6: "the trajectory scheme — today the single second-order `EndpointHeun`, with higher-order schemes the studied future axis"
PAGE: api / Particles, AbstractParticleIntegrator: "Two members today: `EndpointHeun`... and `AdamsBashforth`..."
PAGE: decisions: "(2026-08, user-requested) A second trajectory scheme: variable-step Adams–Bashforth."
findings.contradicts: Architecture §4.6 asserts the trajectory-scheme set has exactly one member and calls a higher-order scheme a future axis; the Particles API page and the decision log record that AdamsBashforth already exists, putting the set at two members.
findings.description: The set is 'trajectory schemes built today.' Architecture claims cardinality one ('the single ... EndpointHeun') and frames higher order as still-future work. The Particles API page and decision log both show the set now has two members (EndpointHeun, AdamsBashforth) — the 'studied future axis' this sentence describes has already been closed. Stale architecture text not updated after the AdamsBashforth addition.

findings.title: advance! claims tracers are always pushed by Heun-in-time
locations: PAGE: api / SimulationRun, advance!: "Advects the tracers, if any, by Heun-in-time on the start- and end-of-step velocities"
PAGE: Home, Components: "Particles: ... second-order `advect!` (Heun-in-time)..."
PAGE: api / SimulationRun, Simulation Arguments: "`trajectory_scheme = EndpointHeun()`... Pass `AdamsBashforth()` when trajectory accuracy in time limits a measurement"
findings.contradicts: advance!'s docstring universally states tracers are advanced by Heun-in-time; the same page's Simulation constructor documents trajectory_scheme as user-selectable with AdamsBashforth (a multistep, not Heun-in-time, scheme) as an explicit alternative.
findings.description: The set is 'runs advance! can drive,' parametrized by trajectory_scheme (2 members: EndpointHeun, AdamsBashforth). The claim 'by Heun-in-time' holds for 1 of 2 and is false for AdamsBashforth. The Home page's parenthetical '(Heun-in-time)' on advect! repeats the same universal overreach.

findings.title: Cached column's 4 stated values never all appear in its own table
locations: PAGE: observables_cache §2.4: "Its Cached column takes four values: yes... `depends`... `no`... and `never`..."
PAGE: observables_cache §2.4, table rows (all ~19): every value shown is yes, no, or never — none is `depends`
findings.description: The set is the table's own rows (checked all ~19). The prose defines and explains a fourth value, `depends` ('the observable survives in some configurations and not in others'), but zero rows in the accompanying table use it, so the only worked example never shows what it looks like. Plausibly deliberate, since §2 fixes one specific configuration ('One configuration fixes the system'), which would preclude any row varying by configuration — hence only medium confidence.

findings.title: UNFALSIFIABILITY: decision 40 re-admits the chart-liveness tautology decision 37 retired
locations: PAGE: decisions, decision 37 — "Extending those and then reporting the result as the bound made the physical-vector cell a tautology"
PAGE: decisions, decision 40 — "`DYNAMICS_LIVE` absorbs the charts as facts of the deposit-persistence contract"
PAGE: decisions, decision 40 — "Every unforced ledger cell now sits at its liveness bound in every class"
findings.contradicts: decision 37: "The observation cache's charts are live because a design choice says so … a different design does not." Axis: may a design contract's liveness enter the lower bound?
findings.description: Decision 37 rules that design-chosen liveness may never enter a lower bound. Decision 40 re-admits the charts into DYNAMICS_LIVE, relabelling the deposit-persistence contract a fact. But the cache page says contents change when the solver's storage decisions change — it is a design choice under a new name. achieved == bound is again true by construction: any schedule releasing the charts would also delete the slots the ledger counts. What observation refutes it? None.
findings.resolution_hint: Either hold the deposit-persistence extension as a named holder, or state what run would make achieved > bound.

findings.title: CIRCULARITY: "caching adds nothing" holds only because the cache's own schedule supplies the "anyway"
locations: PAGE: observables_cache §1.1 — "Caching an observable adds nothing to what an iteration computes, moves, or stores."
PAGE: observables_cache §1.4 — "paid even by a hand-fixed-$\Delta t$ run that never reads the number"
PAGE: api / Observables, `max_speed` — "Under a hand-fixed $\Delta t$ nothing consumes it and the pass is spent anyway"
findings.contradicts: §1.2's admission test "Computed — some component must produce it anyway", against §1.4's admitted per-iteration extra pass.
findings.description: max_speed is cacheable because the iteration computes it anyway; under a fixed step the iteration computes it only because the cache's schedule is fixed at construction. The axiom's "anyway" is thus supplied by the cache itself. §1.4 concedes the extra pass, then asserts "the only work it adds over a cacheless solver is §1.3's final closing deposit, paid once per run" — falsified by its own preceding clause.
findings.resolution_hint: State the axiom as holding under the adaptive-CFL path, and name the fixed-step pass as the design's one admitted cost.

findings.title: INCONSISTENT RULE PAIR: three incompatible mechanisms guard the PhaseShift displaced-velocity reuse
locations: PAGE: decisions, decision 56 — "`prepare!` opens every step with the mark cleared" / "not load-bearing for correctness"
PAGE: api / Generator, `ResolvedGenerator` — "recorded as the identity of the `û` it was taken of rather than either signature"
PAGE: api / Generator, `scalar_rhs!` — "Pass `displaced_velocity_current = true` only if nothing has changed"
findings.contradicts: A freshness mark cleared by prepare! vs a source-identity record vs a caller-supplied keyword — three different deciders for one guard.
findings.description: If the generator records the source û and rebuilds on mismatch, the keyword discriminates nothing. If the keyword decides, the record is inert under its false default and a caller passing true wrongly is silently wrong — contradicting decision 56's "not load-bearing for correctness" and scalar_rhs!'s own "is what makes an unpaired call correct rather than quietly wrong". At most one of the three can be the contract.
findings.resolution_hint: Pick one mechanism and delete the other two descriptions.

findings.title: EQUIVOCATION: `ParticleIntegratorBuffers` names both the per-scheme family and one scheme's concrete registers
locations: PAGE: api / Particles, `ParticleIntegratorBuffers` — "a multistep scheme wants a velocity history and no predicted positions at all — which is why it lives here"
PAGE: api / Particles, `MultistepBuffers` — "The per-scheme registers of an `AdamsBashforth` trajectory integrator"
PAGE: api / Particles, `advect!` — "`buffers` (a `ParticleIntegratorBuffers` built for that scheme)"
PAGE: api / Propagator, `allocate_buffers` — "allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers) -> ParticleIntegratorBuffers"
findings.contradicts: The multistep case is a different type built by a three-argument call, allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers, cache).
findings.description: ParticleIntegratorBuffers is documented as the storage any trajectory scheme gets, with fields (predictor, predictor_points, velocity_predictor) that are Heun's alone, while AdamsBashforth takes MultistepBuffers. So advect!'s documented argument type and allocate_buffers' documented signature and return type are both false for one of the two shipped schemes; architecture §4.6 inherits the same error.
findings.resolution_hint: Name the abstract family separately from EndpointHeun's concrete register set, and document both allocate_buffers arities.

findings.title: The second trajectory scheme exists on the API pages but not in the prose that quantifies over schemes
locations: PAGE: architecture §4.6 — "today the single second-order `EndpointHeun`, with higher-order schemes the studied future axis"
PAGE: api / SimulationRun, `advance!` — "Advects the tracers, if any, by Heun-in-time on the start- and end-of-step velocities"
PAGE: Home, Components — "`Particles`: Lagrangian tracer tracking — second-order advection"
PAGE: api / Particles, `AbstractParticleIntegrator` — "Two members today: `EndpointHeun` … and `AdamsBashforth`"
findings.contradicts: decision 57, "A second trajectory scheme: variable-step Adams–Bashforth", and the `trajectory_scheme = AdamsBashforth()` option on `Simulation`.
findings.description: Three current-state surfaces still assert a single second-order scheme, and advance! states Heun-in-time as a fact rather than as the default — false for a configuration the Simulation docstring advertises. This is a class defect across every surface that quantifies over the trajectory schemes, not a single stale line.
findings.resolution_hint: Sweep §4.6, Home Components, the Particles module map and advance! together, then re-check.

findings.title: Three different module include orders are each stated as the order
locations: PAGE: architecture §4.9 — "`SimulationDomain → Observables → State → Cache → Forcing → …`"
PAGE: api — "in the order `SimulationDomain` → `State` → `Observables` → `Cache` → …"
PAGE: decisions, decision 54 — "The include order becomes `State → Observables → Cache`"
findings.contradicts: §4.9 places Observables before State; the API overview and decision 54 place State first. Axis: the dependency order.
findings.description: Observables and State are swapped between §4.9 and the two other statements. Decision 54 is the entry that set the order and the API overview agrees with it, so §4.9's layout summary is the outlier. This is not the decision-log-as-history case: §4.9 is a current-state section, and the two orders cannot both be the dependency graph.
findings.resolution_hint: Fix §4.9 to match decision 54 and the API overview.

findings.title: NON SEQUITUR: $k$ is excluded from the stationarity gate by a premise false of the default forcing
locations: PAGE: api / SimulationRun, `StationarityCriterion` — "a constant-energy forcing clamps $k$ flat … which is why $k$ is kept out of the gate"
PAGE: api / SimulationRun, `Simulation` — "It does not impose the value step by step as a rescale does, so the fluctuation it leaves is genuine"
findings.contradicts: Axis: clamped vs restored. The default VarianceController restores k exponentially; it does not clamp.
findings.description: The exclusion of k rests on a disjunction: either the forcing clamps k flat, or a fixed-injection forcing makes it ring. Under the shipped default neither disjunct holds as stated — the package's own contrast is that the controller restores rather than clamps. The conclusion may still be right, but the stated reason does not reach the default configuration, and "constant-energy forcing" does double duty for the clamp and the controller.
findings.resolution_hint: Restate the reason in terms the controller satisfies (a held quantity is a poor drift signal, clamped or restored).

findings.title: EQUIVOCATION: `ConstantPower`'s rate is re-solved "each step" and "at every stage" in one docstring
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, `ConstantPower` — "whose rate $A$ is set each step so the field's injection rate holds the `injection_rate`"
PAGE: api / Forcing, `ConstantPower` — "it enters the right-hand side at every stage rather than the integrating factor"
PAGE: api / Forcing, module map — "`ConstantPower` — a band amplitude re-solved each stage"
findings.contradicts: "each step" vs "every stage" for the same quantity, three lines apart, on the axis decision 58 made load-bearing.
findings.description: Decision 58's whole point is that a per-step rate is the first-order routing and a per-stage source the order-preserving one. The identity sentence still says "set each step" — precisely the retired behaviour — while the paragraph below and the module map say stage. A reader deciding whether ConstantPower costs the scheme its order gets both answers from one docstring.
findings.resolution_hint: Change the identity sentence to "re-solved at every stage".

findings.title: EQUIVOCATION on "the state": the cache's kind test versus a cached observable of the positions
locations: PAGE: observables_cache §1.2 — "It must be determined by the state at a single $t_n$ — by the state alone, in every argument."
PAGE: observables_cache §1.1 — "Where this page says the state, it means the fluid's"
PAGE: api / Cache, `ObservablesCache` — "the sample is a function of the state and the positions together"
findings.contradicts: The admission test quantifies over the fluid state alone, yet the particle-velocities slot has a non-state argument and is cached "yes".
findings.description: The kind test is stated as a universal over arguments, then widened by "the probe's position counts as an argument and is bound by the same rule". Under the page's own definition of the state, positions are not the state, so either the test means "each argument is itself at a single t_n" — a weaker, different rule — or the cached particle velocities violate it. One sense of "state" states the rule, another applies it.
findings.resolution_hint: Restate the kind test over "every dynamical factor the quantity reads", not "the state alone".

findings.title: INCONSISTENT RULE PAIR: a CFL ceiling is "a property of the scheme and the grid", except for the value that is not
locations: PAGE: api / Propagator, `recommended_cfl` — "This function takes no $\nu$, by design — a CFL ceiling is a property of the scheme and the grid"
PAGE: api / Propagator, `recommended_cfl` — "`IFRK2`'s margin is the one value that depends on a quantity it cannot see"
findings.contradicts: The definitional claim and its admitted counterexample sit in one paragraph.
findings.description: The design rule is the premise for refusing a viscosity argument, and the next clause concedes that one of the two returned values is not an instance of the rule. Either the rule is normative — in which case IFRK2's 0.25 is a defect to be named rather than a by-design return — or it is descriptive and false. As written the premise is refuted by the function's own output.
findings.resolution_hint: Recast the rule as the intended invariant and mark IFRK2's margin as the recorded violation.

findings.title: VACUOUS DISCRIMINATION: `gain` and `turnover_time` are two settings for one observable quantity
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, `VarianceController` — "Only the ratio $t_\ell/G$ is observable"
PAGE: api / Forcing, `VarianceController` — "The two are kept separate because that is how the source states them."
PAGE: api / Forcing, `VarianceController` — "`gain = 1` — the dimensionless gain $G$. Larger relaxes faster"
findings.description: Two arguments are documented as independent settings, then declared to act only through their ratio: any (G, t_ℓ) with equal ratio is the same controller, so the two-parameter surface discriminates nothing a run can measure. The stated justification — "because that is how the source states them" — is the appeal-to-existing-arrangement ARCHITECTURE §8 rules out ("legacy is not evidence of correctness").
findings.resolution_hint: Either expose the settling time directly, or give a first-principle reason for the split.

findings.title: VACUOUS DISCRIMINATION: the `valid_Reλ` guard excludes nothing by default and no shipped consumer enforces it
locations: PAGE: api / phenomenology / Phenomenology, `Reference` — "`Reference(citation; valid_Reλ = (0.0, Inf))`"
PAGE: api / phenomenology / Phenomenology, `Reference` — "A comparison reads `valid_Reλ` so a law is not judged outside its stated domain"
PAGE: api / phenomenology / StructureFunctions, `Lundgren2002` — "a comparison that honours `valid_Reλ` never evaluates it in the region where the sign flips"
findings.contradicts: decision 51 — "The `validate_spectrum` helper leaves the package altogether" — so the comparer that would honour the range is not shipped.
findings.description: The default range admits every Re_λ, so for any law that does not override it the guard is a no-op. The protection is also stated conditionally ("a comparison that honours valid_Reλ") while the package's only comparer was moved to the test suite. Lundgren2002's sign-flip hazard is therefore guarded by a convention no shipped code applies.
findings.resolution_hint: Say plainly that the range is advisory metadata, and note where enforcement lives.

findings.title: EQUIVOCATION: the skewness gate is "strict"/"decisive" and its default floor is admittedly permissive
locations: PAGE: api / Observables, `derivative_skewness` — "Its plateau is the strict \"real turbulence yet\" gate of the warm-up detector."
PAGE: api / SimulationRun, `StationarityCriterion` — "the decisive \"real turbulence yet\" signal"
PAGE: api / SimulationRun, `StationarityCriterion` — "clearing it means \"no longer Gaussian\", not \"fully developed\""
findings.contradicts: strict/decisive vs a default floor at one fifth of the developed value (decision 20: "whose default floor is a permissive one").
findings.description: One gate is labelled strict and decisive on two surfaces and permissive on a third. "Strict" is separately applied to ε in the same criterion docstring ("a flat ε is the strict indicator"), so the word carries two senses in one paragraph. A reader cannot tell whether a passed warm-up asserts a developed cascade or merely a non-Gaussian field.
findings.resolution_hint: Reserve "strict" for the ε test and describe the skewness gate by what its floor actually certifies.

findings.title: EQUIVOCATION: `set_forcing_rate!` is gated by linearity in one docstring and steadiness in its neighbours
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, `set_forcing_rate!` — "For a strategy `forcing` linear in the field, fill the per-mode rate"
PAGE: api / Forcing, `AbstractForcing` — "decided by steadiness in time, not linearity in the field"
PAGE: api / Forcing, `uses_steady_linear_rate` — "Steady, not merely linear, is the load-bearing word"
findings.contradicts: The hook's identity sentence uses the criterion decision 58 explicitly retired.
findings.description: Two neighbouring docstrings state incompatible admission criteria for one hook. ConstantPower is linear in the field and must not use set_forcing_rate!, so the identity sentence's stated condition is satisfied by a strategy the other two docstrings bar from the hook. The exactness argument then trades silently on the two senses.
findings.resolution_hint: Open set_forcing_rate! with "For a strategy whose per-mode rate is steady in time".

findings.title: NON SEQUITUR: `Kolmogorov1941`'s order guard is justified by a universality its own bullet denies
locations: PAGE: api / phenomenology / StructureFunctions, `Kolmogorov1941` — "any other `order` throws an `ArgumentError` (K41 fixes only these two longitudinal moments universally)"
PAGE: api / phenomenology / StructureFunctions, `Kolmogorov1941` — "the constant $C_2 \approx 2.0$ is empirical"
findings.contradicts: Order 2 is admitted although its amplitude is empirical, while the same law returns ζ_p = p/3 at every p.
findings.description: The guard's reason is that K41 universally fixes only orders 2 and 3. But the order-2 amplitude is explicitly empirical, so it is not universally fixed, and the same law's scaling_exponent is unrestricted in p. The real discriminator is known amplitudes, not universality; as written the reason neither supports admitting order 2 nor explains why the exponents escape the restriction.
findings.resolution_hint: Say the law carries amplitudes only at these two orders, and that exponents are given at every p.

findings.title: The misdeclaration guard covers only one of the two mismatches it is sold as preventing
locations: PAGE: api / Forcing, `uses_steady_linear_rate` — "a forcing that fills a rate without declaring one is never given an array to fill, and the `ResolvedGenerator` constructor rejects it"
PAGE: api / Forcing, `set_forcing_rate!` — "the default method is never reached in a run; it returns `rate` untouched"
findings.contradicts: The opposite mismatch — declaring true without implementing the hook — is exactly the case that reaches the default.
findings.description: The guard is presented as preventing a forcing going silently unapplied, but only the implement-without-declaring direction is checked. A strategy declaring uses_steady_linear_rate and not implementing set_forcing_rate! is handed a rate array, the no-op default returns it untouched, and the run is quietly unforced — the failure the guard claims to prevent. The universal "never reached in a run" holds only under the unchecked half.
findings.resolution_hint: Either check both directions at construction, or qualify the "never reached" claim.

findings.title: The deposit-completeness check cannot fire under its own stated premise
locations: PAGE: observables_cache §1.3 — "the completeness check throws if a slot is still with its epoch cleared"
PAGE: observables_cache §1.3 — "No caller can cause this — a slot exists only because the schedule fills it"
PAGE: observables_cache §1.3 — "The schedule is fixed when the cache is built and runs identically on every iteration"
findings.description: Together the three sentences entail that no reachable run state satisfies the check's condition, making it a claim about the source rather than about the run. The page half-concedes this ("the check guards the solver against itself"), but the surrounding prose presents it as a runtime invariant of the cache.
findings.resolution_hint: Present it as an internal assertion against solver defects, or drop the premise that makes it vacuous.

findings.title: EQUIVOCATION: `Li2008` is an author-year handle for a fit the docstring says is not theirs
locations: PAGE: api / phenomenology / Scalings, `Li2008` — "The value is this package's own reduction of the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (JHTDB)"
PAGE: architecture §4.8 — "the paper is the author-year handle (`Pope2000`, first author's surname …)"
findings.contradicts: The naming rule binds the handle to the paper the parametrization comes from; here the paper supplies the dataset, not the fit.
findings.description: Under the stated three-level convention Li2008 asserts that Li et al. (2008) published this parametrization; the docstring says the number is our own reduction of their dataset. The architecture insists our own fits sit beside the literature on equal footing, so an own-fit deserves an own handle. As it stands one name carries two provenances, and a reader checking G ≈ 0.9 against Li et al. will not find it there.
findings.resolution_hint: Rename to our own author-year handle, citing JHTDB as the data source.

findings.title: "chart" is given two incompatible identity conditions for vorticity
locations: PAGE: notation, §Vocabulary — "chart | a physical-representation view of the spectral state — the velocity, vorticity or scalar recovered from it."
PAGE: architecture, §11 decision log (2026-08, user-directed) — "What remains a package verb is the one recovery that is not a chart: vorticity_physical!"
findings.contradicts: Notation's Vocabulary entry names vorticity as one of the three things a 'chart' is; the later, more specific decision-log entry (and Architecture §4.1, which separates 'the velocity and scalar are recovered by to_physical!' from 'the derived vorticity comes from vorticity_physical!') states the opposite as the settled current design — vorticity recovery is explicitly the one recovery that is NOT a chart, because it is a genuine derived observable (a curl) rather than a representation-preserving view. The Notation page is a current-state reference, not history, so this is a live contradiction, not a stale-decision-log exemption.
findings.description: The document never gives a single identity criterion for 'is X a chart' — the answer for vorticity flips depending which page is consulted. This is load-bearing: 'chart' organizes the cache's field-slot design and the in-place reuse story (decision 47), so a reader relying on the Notation glossary will misclassify vorticity's status relative to the rest of the corpus.

findings.title: Module's own identity says "tracer" where the naming rule requires "particle"
locations: PAGE: Home, §Components — "`Particles`: Lagrangian tracer tracking — second-order advection and field sampling along trajectories…"
PAGE: api (overview) — "Particles: Lagrangian tracer tracking — `Tracers`, second-order `advect!`…"
PAGE: api / Particles (module docstring) — "Particles … Lagrangian tracer tracking:"
PAGE: architecture, §11 decision log (2026-08, user-directed) — "Anything true of the whole deferred ladder of §7 takes particle … only what is specific to the massless … kind takes tracer."
